title: The stamp that found itself
passages:
The Kettering night board ran the length of the west wall, thirty-one screens, eleven rigs posted, four holes where rigs should have been. Kass had the desk terminal open with badge 2241 already in the reader. The channel record keeps the badge of whoever keyed a rig onto the line, and 2241 sat on channel 12-K at 04:51, the minute the fourth ghost rig stopped being anywhere.

They keyed SCRUB.

*KEYED LINES CLOSE FROM THE FAR END.*

"The far end's gone," Kass said.

*FAR END NOT PRESENT. LINE CANNOT CLOSE.*

"Open a discrepancy, then."

*A DISCREPANCY REQUIRES A SECOND KEY.*

They had tried at 02:00 and again at 04:52 and the terminal had said the same three things each time, in the same flat voice, like a man reading a menu he hadn't cooked. Nineteen hours on shift. Their name was going to sit on that channel until the sun went out, and the worst part was that they had keyed it themselves, doing their job, watching a rig delete itself under their own hand.

Boots came in from the yard side at 05:41, unhurried, and stopped at the clock post. Bay 4 coveralls, Shift 2 patch, a face Kass had seen on eleven months of rosters and never once spoken to.

"You're Ospina."

"I'm a loader who'd like to be somewhere else."

"You're Bay 4's seal authority and you walked out of Anza unlogged."

"I walked out of Anza." Ospina put their badge against the post and didn't press. "I'm clocking the oh-six-hundred. Then I'm going home for nine hours and none of this."

"Four rigs came off this board as derelict. Somebody crimped every one of them shut and stamped the plate. There is one seal authority on your shift, and they're standing at my clock post with their hand in their pocket."

Ospina's hand was in their pocket. It stayed there.

"I found that stamp," they said. "In a tool void. I didn't use it. I've now told that to a dispatcher, to a node operator on the open channel, and to you, and it keeps not helping."

"Anza confessed on the open channel an hour ago. Their loader signed the shortfall in front of the whole shop. You heard that from the road, I'd guess."

"I heard it from the road."

"Then you know what a chipped die means when it shows up on a ballast plate." Kass pulled the badge out of the reader and held it, which is not the same as scrubbing it, but it kept the terminal from saying anything else. "A seal authority who misses two boards gets the stamp pulled to the node. You know that. Clock in, keep your die, and then get on a rig with me."

"To Anza." Ospina said it the way you'd say a diagnosis. "Your node's on the record feeding seals down the line. I'm not putting my name inside that."

"Nobody's asking for your name."

"Somebody always is."

Ospina turned to the post, badge up, and Kass had time to think *good, they're going to do it* before the board lit a line nobody had asked for.

*SEAL AUTHORITY LIVE ON FLOOR. BAY FOUR. DIE PRESENT.*

Every clerk in the room looked up. Down at the far end, a man in Bay 4 coveralls stopped walking.

Ospina looked at their own pocket like it had spoken out of turn. "That's not supposed to happen."

"It reads the die, not the badge," Kass said. "You walked a true stamp into a yard that's short one, and you just told every soul on the floor where it is."

The clock over the post said 05:44.

Kass set the badge down on the desk, face up, where they could see it and the terminal couldn't.

"Go home in ten minutes," they said. "I'll walk you to the yard gate myself."

Ospina didn't come off the clock post. "Ten minutes is how long a rig takes to ruin a day."

"It's four records."

They pulled the derelict file. *Derelict* is a line word: a rig that misses two calls isn't lost, isn't stolen, isn't broken. It's derelict, and derelict has a procedure, and the procedure is faster than any of the other three. Kass laid the four side by side on the west wall, one screen each, thirty-one screens and now four of them doing something.

*LK-1180. LK-2266. LK-3071. LK-4519.*

"Read me the wreck report on 1180."

"There isn't one." Ospina came two steps closer, which was two steps more than Kass expected. "No crash line. No scrub line. No tow-in, no shoulder mark, no driver's statement. It just stops answering and then it's on a claim."

Every one of the four had the same three lines under it. A derelict order. A standing reclamation claim. A dispatch.

"Explain the claim to me like I'm a clerk," Kass said, "because I am one."

"A standing claim is an open order that never closes," Ospina said. "Line reclamation keeps a few live forever. Cargo reads as dead weight, an agent gets dispatched, the agent hauls it to a yard and breaks the plate. The discrepancy goes away because the thing making it goes away." They shrugged, unhappy about it. "That's the whole job. Pell's the agent. The fob on his chest is the warrant-token. He can freeze a node's board and its resupply until the node hands over whatever the claim names."

"Four rigs, four claims, one agent."

"Four rigs, four claims." Ospina leaned in and stopped. "Kass. Look at the key line."

Kass looked. Under each claim, the field that records who keyed it: the badge that put the order on the line.

*KEYED: 2241. CHANNEL 12-K.*

"All four."

"I've never keyed a claim," Kass said. "Nineteen months. I key rigs on and rigs off. Claims come down from the line desk with a supervisor's number on them, and I have never once had a supervisor's number."

"Then somebody's wearing yours like a coat." Ospina straightened up. "That's my answer for the four. I can go home."

"There's a fifth."

The fifth claim was open. Not dispatched-and-closed like the others: open, live, pulsing. Destination field, one word. *ANZA.* Target field, a description instead of a number, because there was no number to use.

*UNIT, MEDICAL. NO TRANSPONDER. NOT PRESENT ON ANY BOARD. LAST MASS POSTED: KETTERING NORTH GATE.*

"That's the rig Rhea towed in on a hook," Ospina said. "I was in the yard when it came off the road. Nobody's ever going to find it, it's got no transponder and no plate on the board."

"That's not how it reads from here." Kass tapped the status line. "Anything not on the board reads as derelict. It isn't a judgment, it's a filing status. No board entry, no crew, no cargo, no owner. Free to haul." They scrolled. The dispatch block had a live ETA and a note that the agent was already rolling with his pendant keyed. *AT NODE PRIOR TO 06:00 BOARD.*

Ospina's hand was still in their pocket. It had been in that pocket since 05:41 and Kass was starting to understand it wasn't going to come out for anybody.

"Somebody at Anza confessed on the open channel," Kass said. "Feed the seals down the line, keep the roster fat. And now their ore siding has a rig on it that isn't on any board, and a reclaimer is thirteen minutes out to collect it."

"That's their problem. Their loader signed her own name to it in front of the shop."

Kass scrolled to the bottom of the fifth claim, where the delivery block sits, and turned the screen so Ospina could read it.

*RECEIVED: ANZA. SHIFT ONE. NODE CODE 4-11.*

"Nobody received anything," Ospina said.

"Somebody did," Kass said. "An hour ago. For a rig that isn't on their board."
